title: The Woman Whose Cough Turned to Blood — A Wasting Illness With a Mass on Imaging

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 60 years old, presenting with cough and expectoration along with breathlessness for a month, fever for a month, and vomiting and loose stools for four days. She had been apparently well 20 years earlier, with only an intermittent cough about once a month that responded to medication. A month before this presentation, she developed high-grade fever with chills, low back pain, and breathlessness with cough and expectoration; she was diagnosed with anemia at a hospital at that time and managed with ceftriaxone. Her symptoms worsened over the last four days, with blood in her sputum and wheezing.

She has had vomiting 4–6 times a day for four days, containing food and water without bile or blood, and loose stools 5–6 times a day for the same period, with loss of appetite and significant weight loss (4–5 kg over the week). She denies painful urination, black stools, or headache. She has no history of hypertension, diabetes, epilepsy, thyroid disease, asthma, or tuberculosis, and no prior surgery or transfusions. Her brother had similar complaints and died 25 years ago; her sister has chronic cough and breathlessness and uses inhalers. She reached menarche at 13, married at 14, had regular periods, and reached menopause at 45.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General exam:** conscious, oriented, cooperative; thin build and malnourished; height 158 cm, weight 33 kg, BMI 13.25; pallor, koilonychia, and clubbing present; no icterus, cyanosis, generalized lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema
- **Vitals:** temperature 99.3°F, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg
- **Head-to-toe exam:** temporal wasting; a shiny, bald, bulky, red tongue; a grayish-white patch on the soft palate; wasting of the temporalis and deltoid muscles; ichthyotic skin on the limbs; a firm, mobile 2.5 cm left supraclavicular lymph node; lower thoracic and lumbar kyphoscoliosis; significant lower-limb muscle wasting; and a saddle-nose deformity
- **Respiratory exam:** extensive findings including a deviated trachea, dilated neck and chest wall veins, a barrel-shaped chest, visible left-sided cardiac pulsations, decreased breath sounds and reduced chest expansion on the left, with dullness to percussion and bilateral coarse crackles, most pronounced on the left
- **Abdominal exam:** distended, with an everted umbilicus, distended abdominal veins, shifting dullness, and mild splenomegaly, raising the possibility of portal hypertension
- **Cardiovascular and neurological exam:** heart sounds normal; no focal neurological deficit; deep tendon reflexes brisk (3+) throughout
- **Arterial blood gas:** pH 7.24, pCO2 32 mmHg, pO2 79.3 mmHg, bicarbonate 13.2 mmol/L, consistent with a metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
- **2D echocardiogram:** moderate tricuspid regurgitation with pulmonary artery hypertension, mild mitral and aortic regurgitation, hypokinesia of the LAD and RCA/LCx territories, moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and diastolic dysfunction
- **Imaging:** chest X-ray showed bilateral lung collapse with a possible cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe and mediastinal shift to the right; staging was noted as T3N3M0; a lung biopsy was performed on a mass in the left upper lobe
- **Infectious disease screening:** HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and dengue serology all negative; RT-PCR for COVID-19 negative

**Working diagnosis:** heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, with suspected bronchogenic carcinoma, acute gastroenteritis, and oral candidiasis.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
She was started on nebulized bronchodilator therapy and supportive medication with head-end elevation. Over the following days she had intermittent fever spikes with fluctuating hemoptysis, and her vomiting and diarrhea gradually settled. She was maintained on nebulized bronchodilators, vitamin E and B-complex supplementation, and an expectorant syrup, with temperature monitored regularly.

By around day 9, given persistent fever and declining blood pressure, IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) were added; nebulized steroids were introduced shortly after. Her fever gradually subsided over the following days while she continued on IV antibiotics and supportive respiratory care, and by day 13 her cough and fever were both subsiding, with her lung biopsy results informing ongoing management of her suspected malignancy.
